rashi:a1.1: To include its milk: that it is forbidden. And we do not say [that the phrase comes] to include one who slaughters it outside, that he is liable, because if so we would have had to say [that it speaks of a blemish] on the cornea of the eye; and furthermore, the latter clause below teaches: “One who slaughters them outside is exempt.” And the principle of the former clause was not needed to include its milk as permitted: since even its offspring, which is like its own body, as a fetus is a limb of its mother, is now permitted, all the more so its milk, which is mere liquid.
rashi:a2.1: But blemished ones may be redeemed: those that were conceived before the redemption and born after the redemption, where for example he dedicated them for some offering, so that their sanctity is strong enough to transfer to their redemption. And when he dedicates them for an offering, he does not dedicate them as any offering he desires; but for that same offering, he does dedicate them. “How can you find it” is an explanation; that is, how can you find the resolution of the matter, which implies that blemished ones are redeemed and that he may not dedicate them for another offering? Rather, how does he do it? He dedicates them for the sake of that same offering, and they are redeemed in their blemish when a blemish befalls them.
rashi:a3.1: Shall we say this is a refutation of Rav Huna: who said above [15b] that one gathers them into a chamber and they die.
rashi:a4.1: And since the former clause taught “they may be redeemed unblemished”: for it is a novelty that even unblemished ones are redeemed.
rashi:a5.1: And one who slaughters them outside is exempt: the latter clause of the baraita above refers to sacrificial animals whose consecration preceded their blemish, and even so he is exempt, since one is liable for slaughter outside only for what is acceptable inside. As we learned in Zevaḥim, in the chapter Parat Ḥatat (Zevaḥim 112a): “Blemished animals, whether with permanent or temporary blemishes, that one offered outside: he is exempt.” And it derives the reason from the verse “and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting”: whatever is not fit to come to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, one is not liable for it.
rashi:a5.2: Rav Huna teaches “liable”: [in the baraita,] as the mishna [14a] teaches.
rashi:a5.3: And he establishes it as a blemish on the cornea of the eye: which is accepted inside [if it was brought up].
rashi:a5.4: And in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who says: in [the order of] the slaughter of sacrificial animals, in the chapter HaMizbe’aḥ Mekaddesh (Zevaḥim 84a), “if they ascended they shall not descend.” Dukin: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), as in “who stretches out the heavens like a film [dok]” (Isaiah 40:22). And they do not descend because their blemish is not so noticeable. So we learned in Zevaḥim, in the chapter HaMizbe’aḥ Mekaddesh (84a): “Rabbi Akiva deems blemished animals fit,” that is, if they ascended they do not descend; and Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the Gemara there: Rabbi Akiva deemed fit only those with a blemish on the cornea of the eye, since such birds are fit, and only where their consecration preceded their blemish. Another explanation: dukin is a blemish on the eyelids, and the eyelids are called dok because they lie over the eye like the firmament. For so we say in the Sifrei: The parts of the eye resemble a small world: the eyelids correspond to the firmament, the lower one to the earth, the white that surrounds the eye to the ocean that encircles the world, and the round black within it resembles the orb of the sun.
rashi:a6.1: Deferred sanctity: since they had already been redeemed.
tosafot:a6.1: In brief: And its substitute after its redemption dies. If you ask: how is this different from offspring conceived and born after their mother’s redemption, which we counted above [15b] like the offspring of a gazelle or a hart [i.e., non-sacred]? Answer: offspring have sanctity only by force of their mother, and once she is redeemed her sanctity lapses entirely, as with a gazelle or a hart; the remaining prohibition of shearing and labor is too minor to make sanctity take effect on the offspring. But the sanctity of a substitute is different: since the verse revealed that it takes effect even on [an animal with] a permanent blemish, it likewise takes effect after redemption, only it is not sacrificed. A substitute made before redemption is sacrificed, and so it is superior to offspring born before redemption, which according to one opinion above are for grazing. So too Rashi’s wording below (“from where is it derived that the substitute of disqualified consecrated animals dies”: “for example after their redemption, since it cannot be sacrificed”). And the verse “of them that chew the cud” is needed below for a negative mitzva, since by reasoning we already knew it is not sacrificed, as Rav Naḥman says here; and it says the same below of the five sin offerings. Alternatively, verse and reasoning are both needed: without the verse I would say the substitute is not sanctified at all, like a gazelle and a hart, like offspring conceived and born after redemption; and without the reasoning I would say it grazes, reading the verse’s “it is impure” as “wait until it becomes impure,” i.e., blemished, as Rashi explains below. And Rav Amram’s objection, “let it be eaten in its blemish by the owners,” is aimed at Rav Naḥman’s reasoning. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a7.1: And let it be eaten in its blemish: let them wait until it becomes blemished, and let it be eaten by the owners, like a firstborn and a tithe animal, which are not redeemed but are eaten in their blemish. Evidently, since [their substitutes] cannot be sacrificed, as it says in tractate Temura (5b), “Only the firstborn of an ox…”: they are sacrificed, but their substitutes are not sacrificed, and they are eaten in their blemish by the owners. Here too, let it be done so.
rashi:a9.1: But this animal’s sanctity is not strong enough to transfer to its redemption: therefore it dies.
rashi:a10.1: From where is it derived that the substitute of disqualified consecrated animals dies: for example, where after the consecrated animals were redeemed he made a substitute for them, which cannot be sacrificed.
rashi:a10.2: Of them that chew the cud … it is impure: for at the end of the verse it is written “it is impure to you,” and we expound it thus: you have something that has the signs of purity and is forbidden to eat. Which is it? The substitute of disqualified consecrated animals.
rashi:a10.3: Five sin offerings: they are explained in Temura (21b).
rashi:a11.1: For the substitute of a guilt offering: that it grazes. For a guilt offering is not brought as a voluntary offering, so its substitute is not sacrificed. And the verse’s “impure” means: leave it until it becomes “impure,” that is, until a blemish befalls it.
rashi:a12.1: Whatever in a sin offering dies: and the substitute of a sin offering is one of the five sin offerings that die.
rashi:a13.1: There is no negative mitzva: he does not transgress a negative mitzva.
rashi:a13.2: That there is a negative mitzva: “These you shall not eat, of them that chew the cud.”
rashi:a14.1: And if you wish, say: this is why “of them that have a split hoof” comes, which speaks of the sin offerings that die: to juxtapose an item that comes from “them that chew the cud,” namely the substitute of disqualified consecrated animals after their redemption, which is derived from “them that chew the cud,” with an item that comes from “them that have a split hoof,” namely the sin offerings that die.
rashi:a15.1: MISHNA. One who receives tzon barzel: where a gentile valued his animals for him at fixed prices, [the Jew undertaking] to pay him those prices within up to ten years, whether they died or dropped in value; and the offspring they have until that time will be divided between them.
tosafot:a10.1: The verse states: “Of them that chew the cud.” And as for what we expound in the first chapter (above, 6a), “you have something that chews the cud and yet you do not eat it, such as a kosher animal born of a non-kosher one”: there it expounds the beginning of the verse, “Nevertheless these you shall not eat,” and here it expounds the end of the verse, “it is impure to you.” Alternatively, two verses are written.
tosafot:a11.1: Rather, when the verse came, it was for the substitute of a guilt offering: and this is the meaning of the baraita: from where is it derived that the five sin offerings die, and that their counterparts in a guilt offering graze? And “it is impure” means that it grazes until it becomes unfit [through a blemish], as Rashi explained.
tosafot:a12.1: Whatever in a sin offering dies, in a guilt offering grazes: Rabbeinu Tam says that the grazing is rabbinic, and because the Sages instituted grazing, it says everywhere “in a guilt offering it grazes.” But the halakha by Torah law is this: whatever in a sin offering dies, in a guilt offering is sacrificed as a burnt offering, as it says in Pesaḥim at the end of the chapter Elu Devarim (Pesaḥim 73a): a guilt offering that was set aside to graze, and he slaughtered it, is fit as a burnt offering. And there I explained it.
gershom:a1.1: But blemished ones may be redeemed: evidently they are subject to redemption. And “for that same offering he may dedicate them” also implies they are subject to redemption, even unblemished. And that is a double refutation of Rav Huna, who said they die, since they could not come to redemption in any way.
gershom:a2.1: Since it taught the former clause, it taught the latter clause, and the latter clause is not precise.
gershom:a3.1: And this “one who slaughters them outside is exempt” is puzzling: it does not seem to refer back to the baraita or to the mishna. That baraita did not speak of one who slaughters them outside; and if it refers to the mishna, to the case “but if their consecration preceded their blemish,” it should have said “one who slaughters them outside is liable.” So there is no way to establish what it refers to. But my teacher told me: it is reasonable that it refers to the baraita, to what the Gemara said: the principle of the former clause comes to include one who slaughters them outside, that he is exempt.
gershom:a4.1: And Rav Huna teaches “liable,” and establishes this where their consecration preceded their blemish, with a blemish on the cornea of the eye, which is not visible openly like other blemishes.
gershom:a5.1: And in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who says in tractate Zevaḥim: if they ascended they shall not descend. And since, as regards the altar, if they ascended they do not descend, when one slaughters them outside he is liable.
gershom:a6.1: It comes by force of deferred sanctity: since they were made a substitute after redemption.
gershom:a7.1: Its mother’s name is upon it: he calls “its mother” the animal by whose force it comes [i.e., the animal for which it was substituted].
gershom:a8.1: Just as a firstborn and a tithe animal are eaten in their blemish by the owners: for a firstborn without a blemish, its sacrificial portions are offered on the altar, and the priest does not eat them; and when a blemish arises in it, it is eaten entirely by the priest. A tithe animal without a blemish is brought up to Jerusalem and the Israelite himself eats it, and he offers its sacrificial portions on the altar;
gershom:a9.1: and when a blemish arises in it, it is eaten entirely by the Israelite. And “by the owners” taught here does not mean one owner; rather, each as it is: this one by its owners and that one by its owners.
gershom:a10.1: “Of them that chew the cud … impure”: that is, there is an animal that has the signs of purity and is forbidden; that is the substitute of blemished animals after their redemption.
gershom:a11.1: It was needed for the substitute of a guilt offering, which does not die but grazes, so that it be forbidden.
gershom:a12.1: And had it been from the halakha alone, I would say that where one happened to eat, etc.; it teaches us that there is a negative mitzva, as it is written “these you shall not eat.” Another version: since there is a halakha, why is the verse needed? To place it under a positive mitzva, as it is written “that you shall eat” [Leviticus 11:3], and you have another animal with a split hoof that is under a “not” if he offered it [the wording here is unclear], namely the five sin offerings; and a negative derived from a positive statement has the force of a positive mitzva. And the latter version is the more reasonable, for so too we read in Temura, in the chapter Elu Kodashim: “And why was the verse needed? So that if he offers it, he stands in violation of a positive mitzva.” And if you wish, say: the five sin offerings do not need a verse; rather, it is to juxtapose an item that comes from “them that chew the cud,” that is, the substitute of blemished animals, with an item that comes from “them that have a split hoof,” that is, the five sin offerings, which are derived from there: just as there the five sin offerings die, so too the substitute of blemished animals that were redeemed. And this is in accordance with Rav Naḥman.
gershom:a13.1: One who receives tzon barzel from a gentile: that is, he receives an animal from him, binding himself with an obligation as hard as iron [barzel]; for example, the Jew took upon himself that if its value falls or it dies, he will pay the gentile what it is valued at now, and if it bears offspring, the offspring will be between the two of them.
rashi:b1.1: Their offspring are exempt: from the firstborn.
rashi:b1.2: Their offspring: of those tzon barzel animals, when they grow up and give birth for the first time, are exempt from the firstborn. The reason is explained in the Gemara: since if he does not pay the gentile money, he seizes the animal, and if he does not find the animal he seizes the offspring, it turns out that the gentile’s hand is involved in their mother.
rashi:b1.3: And the offspring of offspring are obligated: the offspring of the offspring of the tzon barzel that fall to the Jew’s share, when they have offspring, the firstborns [are given to the priest]; that is, the fourth generation of the tzon barzel is given to the priest.
rashi:b1.4: He established offspring in place of their mothers: he opened a door for the gentile to have a claim on the offspring, and said to him: If the animals die, take the offspring that fall to my share, and they will be in my hands for those same sums until that same time.
rashi:b1.5: And their offspring: now the gentile’s hand is stronger and reaches one more generation; therefore the offspring of those offspring, which are the offspring of the offspring of the tzon barzel, are exempt, since the gentile’s hand reaches them, and when they have a firstborn it is not given to the priest.
rashi:b1.6: Since their liability is to the gentile: for whatever the gentile finds, he always seizes.
tosafot:b1.1: He established offspring in place of their mothers: Rashi explained that he opened a door for him to have a claim on the offspring, and said to him: If the animals die, take the offspring that fall to my share, and it will be in my hands for those sums. And this is clearly implied in the Gemara, as I explained there [below, on 16b]. But in the Tosefta it teaches: “The mothers died and he established the offspring.”
rashi:b3.1: GEMARA. Since the gentile did not take the money: they stand in the gentile’s possession.
gershom:b4.1: Is that to say: that it stands in the possession of its owner, the gentile, and that is why it is exempt from the firstborn.
rashi:b4.1: Stands in the recipient’s possession: for it is the recipient who is obligated for the money, and what the giver takes, half the offspring, he takes as payment for waiting for the money. For if the animals stood in the owner’s possession, why would it be interest? The offspring grew in their owner’s possession.
tosafot:b4.1: In brief: One may not accept tzon barzel from a Jew because it is interest (Bava Metzia 70b). Rashi there explained: interest, since he valued them for him in money, and as long as he has not paid his money they split the profit; and although the mishna seems superfluous, since it already taught that one may not set up a shopkeeper for half the profit (all the more so here, where he took all the liability), it is stated for the sake of the latter clause, that one may accept tzon barzel from gentiles, teaching that interest from gentiles is permitted. Difficulty for Rashi: what does our Gemara ask, “if it stood in the owner’s possession, why is it interest”? Even so it would be rabbinic interest: with all the liability on the recipient it is a loan and the owner takes half the gain for the loan, and it is not Torah interest only because if there is no gain he takes nothing. Rather, as Rabbeinu Tam explained, it is Torah interest: he fixed a price for the flock and a price for the gain and undertook to pay every year whether there is gain or not, which is fixed interest; and this mishna teaches that it is Torah interest, beyond the shopkeeper case, which is rabbinic. (Tosafot discusses here Bava Metzia 64b, “one who lends to his fellow may not live in his courtyard for free … because it is interest,” which Rabbeinu Tam explains as rabbinic; but here “because it is interest” must mean Torah interest, or what would it teach?) The Yerushalmi supports Rabbeinu Tam: “What is tzon barzel? He had a hundred sheep and said: they are charged to you at a hundred gold dinars; the offspring, milk and wool are yours; if they die you are responsible; and you pay me a sela for each one from your own” — the last is forbidden, clearly fixing both principal and gain. Without the interest mishna, our mishna would pose no difficulty: the animals would rightly count as in the gentile’s possession, since if unpaid he seizes the animal, or else the offspring, all being pledged to him for the principal. But once it is Torah interest, it has left the owner’s possession entirely like any loan; so Rava concludes that the exemption is not because it is in the owner’s possession but because the hand of a gentile is in the middle through his lien. If you ask: how is this different from an animal held for the arnona tax, which is obligated in the firstborn according to the first version of Rava in Pesaḥim (6a), where the Jew can pay off [the official] with money; here too, if he pays, the gentile does not seize the offspring? Answer: there the animal belonged to the Jew from the start and is only pledged for the arnona, and since he can pay it off it has not left his possession, so it is not “a gentile’s hand in the middle.” Here it belonged to the gentile from the start, and as long as he keeps the power to seize the animal if unpaid, it has not left his possession and is called “a gentile’s hand in the middle,” since his hand has not been entirely removed. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: And the offspring: what those tzon barzel animals bear is exempt from the firstborn, because half of them belong to the gentile; and also because we say in the Gemara that if he does not find the animal, he seizes its offspring.
gershom:b2.1: The offspring of offspring: the offspring of the offspring are obligated in the firstborn, in the Jew’s share, for the gentile does not go so far as to seize the offspring of offspring on its account.
gershom:b3.1: He established the offspring in place of their mothers: that if the animal dies, the gentile will take the offspring in its place. Those offspring are like the flock [itself], so that what they bear is exempt from the firstborn; the offspring of their offspring are obligated. Rabbi Shimon, etc. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads Rabbi Shimon here.]
gershom:b5.1: One may not accept tzon barzel from a Jew: on the same terms I explained above.
gershom:b6.1: Because it is interest: since he takes upon himself all the liability for the animal, what he gives the owner, half the offspring, is interest. Another version: since he valued the mothers at a price and gives him half the offspring, this is interest, for it implies that he gives them to him for waiting for the money.
gershom:b7.1: Evidently it stands in the possession of the recipient: the animal; for if it stood in the giver’s possession, it gave birth in his possession and it would not be interest.
rashi:b5.1: [Our] mishna: is where the gentile took upon himself accident and depreciation.
gershom:b8.1: It is not difficult: our mishna stands in the gentile’s possession, and so is exempt from the firstborn, for this reason: that the gentile took upon himself accident and depreciation of the animal.
gershom:b9.1: And here, regarding a Jew, the recipient took upon himself accident and depreciation; therefore it is interest.
rashi:b6.1: If he took upon himself accident and depreciation, do you call it tzon barzel? Asked in astonishment: tzon barzel is only where the recipient takes the accident upon himself, for that is why you call it “iron”: it is hard and does not diminish; so too for the giver, he will receive no less than its value.
rashi:b6.2: And furthermore, why the unqualified statement? Asked in astonishment: that is, it states the matter without qualification, although there is a distinction between one tzon barzel and another.
rashi:b7.1: Instead of teaching the latter clause: there [in Bava Metzia], “but one may accept, etc.”
gershom:b10.1: Let it distinguish within it: in the case of one who receives from a Jew, that sometimes one may accept and sometimes one may not: “In what case is this said, etc.” And why did it need to teach “but one may accept from a gentile”? Even from a Jew [one may, in such a case].
rashi:b8.1: Rather: both this and that are where the owner did not take accident and depreciation upon himself, but everything is on the recipient.
gershom:b11.1: Both this and that: both the mishna in Bekhorot and the mishna in Bava [Metzia] are where the giver did not take it upon himself.
rashi:b8.2: And here, regarding the firstborn: it is not because it is in the gentile’s possession, but because it is held as a pledge for him.
gershom:b12.1: And here: what is the reason it is exempt from the firstborn? Because if the gentile comes, etc.
rashi:b9.1: Rav Huna said: the offspring of tzon barzel are exempt, etc.: as I explained on the mishna; and this refers to the first clause.
gershom:b13.1: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda disagree about the first clause of the mishna, “one who receives tzon barzel from a gentile.”
rashi:b9.2: Rav Yehuda says: the offspring of offspring are also exempt: and the fourth generation of the tzon barzel he does not give to the priest, only the fifth. And below [17a] the Gemara raises a difficulty against him from the mishna.
gershom:b14.1: The offspring of offspring are also exempt: for he infers this from the wording of the mishna in that matter, as I marked with dots on the page, like an erasure, in the explanation of the mishna.
rashi:b10.1: The reason is that he established: that he strengthened the gentile’s claim; but if he did not establish, the offspring of the offspring of the tzon barzel are not exempt.
tosafot:b10.1: In brief: The reason is that he established, but if he did not establish, no: a refutation of Rav Yehuda. It is puzzling: below [17a] the Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda from the mishna’s explicit words, “the offspring are exempt and the offspring of offspring are obligated,” and answers: read “they and their offspring are exempt,” meaning that the offspring of the tzon barzel are like the tzon barzel themselves, and their offspring, the offspring of offspring, are exempt from giving their young, the fourth generation, to the priest; and though the mishna does not say “they,” it must be obvious to the Gemara that the offspring of tzon barzel are like the tzon barzel themselves. If so, why not explain here too that when the mothers died and he established the offspring in their place, the offspring themselves became tzon barzel, so that “the offspring of offspring are exempt” means one generation further, while without establishing that generation is obligated [and Rav Yehuda would not be refuted]? Answer: that is why Rashi explained in the mishna that “established” does not literally mean that the mothers died and he set the offspring in their place, but that he opened a door for the gentile that if the mothers die the offspring will stand in their place. Alternatively, even if it speaks of where they died, as the Tosefta implies, this is not a full establishing, since he made no act of acquisition in the offspring but merely relied on them for him by word alone. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b15.1: If he established, yes: when he established, he adds another generation to the exemption; but if he did not establish, he does not add another generation.
rashi:b11.1: And this teaches us: that although he established, since it is the gentile’s way to go and seize her young. That is, you might have thought that since the gentile’s claim returns onto the offspring, they should be exempt forever; it teaches us that even so, the offspring of those offspring, which are the offspring of the offspring of the tzon barzel, are exempt, and the offspring of the offspring of the offspring are obligated, as though he had not established.
gershom:b16.1: He said to him: the same is true even though he did not establish; the offspring of offspring are exempt, as I said. And when it teaches “established,” it teaches us a novelty: that although he established, giving him a designated pledge [apotiki], even so, if he does not find the one he established, he seizes her young, that is, the offspring of offspring; therefore they are exempt, since their liability is to the gentile, that is, he seizes even the tenth generation in its place.
rashi:b13.1: We learned: Rabban Gamliel says, etc. [Rashi’s text reads Rabban Gamliel]: and it now enters our mind that he refers to the first clause.
rashi:b13.2: Granted according to Rav Yehuda, who says the first tanna descended: to exempting generations, for the first tanna exempts two generations of the tzon barzel.
gershom:b17.1: Granted according to Rav Yehuda, who says the first tanna descended to generations: that he exempts two generations and obligates the third; for that reason Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel too uses the language of many generations.
